title: How to Keep a Conversation Going: Tips and Questions
h1: How to Keep a Conversation Going: 10 Easy Techniques and Questions to Use
description: Learn how to keep a conversation going in person or over text with easy techniques, open-ended questions and ways to handle awkward silences calmly.
keyword: how to keep a conversation going
excerpt: Practical techniques, ready-to-use questions and calm ways to handle silence so your conversations flow naturally, on dates and everywhere else.
intro:
You've broken the ice, said hello, maybe traded names, and now there's a pause. Your mind goes blank. What do you say next? If that moment makes you tense, you're in good company. Starting a conversation is one skill; keeping it going is another, and it's one almost anyone can learn.

The good news is that great conversationalists aren't necessarily the funniest or most interesting people in the room. They're curious, they listen well, and they give the other person something to work with. Below you'll learn how to keep a conversation going with ten simple techniques, a bank of questions you can borrow, tips for texting, and a calmer way to think about silence. Use them on dates, at parties, at work or anywhere you want to connect.
body:
Why conversations stall

Most conversations run out of steam for a few predictable reasons:

  • Closed questions. "Did you have a good weekend?" can be answered with "Yeah." End of road.
  • One-word answers. When you reply with "Cool" or "Nice," the other person has nothing to build on.
  • Too much self-monitoring. If you're busy worrying about what to say next, you miss the hooks the other person is handing you.
  • Interview mode. Rapid-fire questions without sharing anything back can feel like an interrogation.

Each technique below fixes one of these problems.

10 techniques to keep a conversation going

1. Ask open-ended questions

Open-ended questions start with how, what, why or tell me about. Instead of "Do you like your job?" try "What's the most interesting part of your job?" Instead of "Was the trip fun?" try "What was the highlight of your trip?" These invite stories, and stories give you material for follow-ups.

2. Follow the thread

The easiest next question is usually hidden in their last answer. If they say "I just got back from visiting my sister in Denver," you have three threads: the trip, the sister, Denver. Pick one: "Are you two close?" or "What did you do while you were there?"

3. Give a genuine compliment

A specific, sincere compliment can warm up a conversation and open a new topic. "That's a great jacket, where did you find it?" or "You explained that really clearly; do you teach?" Focus on choices and skills rather than looks, especially with someone you've just met.

4. Share something about yourself

Conversation is a two-way exchange. After they answer, offer a related story or opinion of your own, then hand it back. This balance, sometimes called give-and-take, builds trust and keeps things from feeling like an interview.

5. Find common ground

Shared interests are conversational fuel. Listen for overlaps: a favorite show, a hometown, a hobby, a pet. When you find one, lean in. "Wait, you hike too? What's your favorite trail?" Common ground creates instant rapport.

6. Use the SOFTEN approach for body language

What you do with your body matters as much as what you say. SOFTEN is an easy acronym for friendly nonverbal cues:

  • Smile warmly.
  • Open posture: uncrossed arms, relaxed shoulders.
  • Forward lean, slightly, to show interest.
  • Touch, only when appropriate and welcome, such as a handshake.
  • Eye contact, steady but not staring.
  • Nod to show you're following.

These signals tell the other person you're engaged, which makes them want to keep talking.

7. Listen more than you plan

Active listening means focusing on what they're saying rather than rehearsing your reply. Reflect back what you hear: "So you switched careers after ten years? That's a big leap." People open up when they feel understood.

8. Be genuine

Pretending to love a band you've never heard of will catch up with you. It's fine to say, "I don't know much about that. What got you into it?" Curiosity is more engaging than fake expertise.

9. Don't panic about silence

A pause isn't a failure. In comfortable conversations, people take a breath, sip a drink, or think. Instead of rushing to fill the gap, smile and let it sit for a moment. Then you can return to an earlier topic: "Going back to what you said about learning to surf..."

10. Practice regularly

Think of each chat as a rep, not a test.

Conversation is a skill, and skills improve with reps. Chat with a barista, ask a coworker about their weekend, talk to a neighbor. Low-stakes practice makes high-stakes conversations, like first dates, feel easier.

Tip: Keep three "go-to" topics in your back pocket: something you're looking forward to, something you've recently watched or read, and a light question about their week. They're perfect for restarting a stalled chat.

Questions that keep the conversation flowing

Borrow these when you need a spark. They work best as follow-ups, not a checklist.

Light and easy

  • What's been the best part of your week so far?
  • What do you usually do to unwind on weekends?
  • What's a show or podcast you've been into lately?
  • What's the best thing you've eaten recently?

Getting to know them

  • What's something you're excited about right now?
  • How did you get into what you do?
  • What's a place you'd love to travel to and why?
  • What's a skill you'd love to learn?

A little deeper

  • What's something most people don't know about you?
  • What's a small thing that always makes your day better?
  • Who's had the biggest influence on you?
  • What's a goal you're quietly working toward?

For bigger lists, see our questions to ask on a date and get to know me questions.

How to keep a conversation going over text

Texting has its own rhythm, but the same principles apply.

  • Reply with substance. Add a detail or a question, not just "haha."
  • Reference earlier messages. "How did that presentation go?" shows you remember.
  • Use photos and voice notes. A picture of your terrible latte art can start a whole new thread.
  • Match their pace. If they reply every few hours, you don't need to answer in seconds.
  • Know when to wrap up. Ending on a high note ("Gotta run, but tell me about the concert tomorrow!") leaves both of you wanting more.

For starter ideas, read how to start a conversation with a guy over text.

Tips if you're shy

Shyness doesn't mean you can't be a great conversationalist. In fact, shy people are often excellent listeners.

  • Lead with questions. They take pressure off you and put the spotlight on the other person.
  • Prepare a few stories. Have two or three short anecdotes ready about your work, a recent trip or a funny moment.
  • Set small goals. Aim for one five-minute conversation a day, then build up.
  • Be kind to yourself. Everyone has awkward moments. Most people don't notice yours nearly as much as you do.
Tip: If you blank, simply describe what's around you: "This place has the best playlist" or "Have you tried anything on this menu before?" Your surroundings are an endless source of easy topics.

Conversation habits to avoid

  • One-upping. Matching every story with a bigger one makes people feel unheard.
  • Checking your phone. It signals that you'd rather be elsewhere.
  • Interrupting. Let them finish, even if you're excited.
  • Heavy topics too soon. Save politics, exes and money worries for when you know each other better.
  • Constant complaining. A little venting is relatable; nonstop negativity drains energy.
  • Correcting small details. Interrupting a good story to fix the date or a name breaks the flow. Let minor errors slide.

If you notice yourself doing any of these, don't panic. Simply turn the focus back to the other person with a question about what they were saying.

The bottom line

Learning how to keep a conversation going comes down to curiosity and generosity. Ask open questions, follow the threads, share a little about yourself, and let pauses be pauses. The more you practice, the more natural it feels, and the more people will look forward to talking with you. For more connection tips, explore our dating advice.
takeaways: Open-ended questions that start with how, what or why invite stories and follow-ups.
The best next question is usually hidden in the other person's last answer.
Balance asking with sharing so the chat doesn't feel like an interview.
Friendly body language and active listening keep people talking.
Silence isn't failure; pause, smile and return to an earlier topic.

faq.q: How do you keep a conversation going without it being awkward?
faq.a: Ask open-ended questions, follow up on details they mention, and share related experiences of your own. Keep relaxed body language and don't rush to fill every pause. Awkwardness usually fades when you focus on curiosity instead of performance. Curiosity is contagious.

faq.q: What do you talk about when you run out of things to say?
faq.a: Return to an earlier topic, comment on your surroundings, or ask about something they're looking forward to. Light questions about recent shows, food, travel or weekend plans are reliable restarts that most people enjoy answering. Their answers will hand you the next thread.

faq.q: How do I keep a text conversation going?
faq.a: Reply with a detail or question instead of a one-word answer, reference things they said earlier, and mix in photos or voice notes. Match their texting pace and end on a high note so you both look forward to the next exchange.

faq.q: Is silence bad in a conversation?
faq.a: Not at all. Short pauses are natural and give both people a moment to think. A calm smile during silence feels confident. If the pause stretches, gently pick up a previous thread or ask a new open-ended question. Comfortable silence is often a sign of ease.
